AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI
November 09, 2026 8:00 am EST
Download as PDF
5th Gen AMD EPYC processors power Google Cloud TPU 8tx host infrastructure, helping enterprises protect sensitive AI models
News Highlights:
5th Gen AMD EPYC server CPUs power the host foundation for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
AMD EPYC processors enable protection of sensitive AI models and data, combining host processing, security capabilities and x86 software compatibility.
AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice across more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  09, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced that 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors are powering the host infrastructure for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system to deliver hardware-enforced confidential computing. The expanded collaboration between the companies combines AMD EPYC™ CPU performance, AMD Infinity Guard security capabilities and x86 software compatibility with Google Cloud TPU AI acceleration to help enterprises deploy inference, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning workloads.
1
With Google Cloud’s confidential computing architecture on TPU 8tx supported by 5th Gen AMD EPYC host processors, organizations can run their most sensitive AI workloads at scale in the cloud without compromising on data protection.
The deployment extends the role of AMD EPYC processors as a foundation for accelerated AI infrastructure. Across systems built with GPUs and custom accelerators, AMD EPYC CPUs are the choice for host processing – preparing data, coordinating workloads and managing communication with accelerators. With TPU 8tx, AMD and Google Cloud bring those capabilities together with hardware-rooted security to address a critical requirement for production AI: protecting data while it is in use.
“The most capable AI systems need a CPU foundation that can match the demands of the accelerators they host,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “Across generations of EPYC, we have built leadership capabilities in the performance, memory bandwidth and I/O that keep accelerated systems productive, backed by years of engineering collaboration with the world’s leading cloud providers. Our work with Google Cloud brings that strength to TPU 8tx, helping customers scale AI with the performance and protection their most important workloads demand.”
“When teams move AI agents into production, they need confidence that their data and intellectual property stay private, even from the underlying infrastructure,” said Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager for AI and Computing Infrastructure, Google Cloud. “By pairing 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors with our 8th-generation TPU architecture inside the AI Hypercomputer, we are bringing hardware-enforced confidential computing to cloud TPUs for the first time. Customers get silicon-level data protection alongside the low-latency performance needed for modern reasoning models.”
Enabling Confidential AI with AMD EPYC Processors
In TPU 8tx systems, 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors manage workload orchestration, data preparation and high-throughput communication with TPU accelerators. The system utilizes the AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) capabilities in the AMD EPYC CPU, which together with the TPU, extends confidential computing protection beyond the CPU to connected accelerators, helping protect sensitive data as it moves among them.
Verifying an accelerator’s identity and security configuration before granting it direct access to protected memory helps customer prompts, model weights and intermediate data remain encrypted in CPU memory and in transit among the host and accelerators, with hardware isolation during accelerator execution. These protections help enterprises use sensitive information with confidence in reasoning and agentic AI applications.
AMD EPYC processors also underpin the broader Google Cloud confidential computing portfolio: AMD SEV technologies help protect workloads across Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, Confidential Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Confidential Dataflow. TPU 8tx extends that collaboration to confidential AI acceleration.
A Proven Host CPU Foundation Across AI Architectures
As hyperscalers, frontier labs and model providers build increasingly specialized AI infrastructure, CPU selection remains central to system performance and deployment. Accelerators depend on host processors to supply data, schedule work and connect AI workloads with the applications and services around them. AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice for more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
AMD EPYC processors support this role across systems using AMD Instinct™ GPUs, Nvidia GPUs and custom silicon. This breadth gives customers a proven CPU platform across accelerator choices, supported by the established x86 software ecosystem.
Building on Generations of AMD and Google Cloud Collaborations
AMD and Google Cloud have collaborated across multiple generations of EPYC processors, supporting general-purpose, compute-intensive, storage-intensive and accelerated workloads leading up to current Google Cloud Compute Engine C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D and G4 virtual machines. The companies have also worked together for years on security technology at the corporate level, including deep reviews of AMD security processor firmware by Google security experts.
With TPU 8tx, this expanded collaboration helps enterprises run modern reasoning and agentic AI workloads in production without compromising on data protection.

We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our
AI for Science program
, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.
We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted
Team plan for scientists
and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.
Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with
HHMI Janelia Research Campus
to develop the
Model Hardware Standard
(MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the
Allen Institute
, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.
Science funders and societies
Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
The Simons Foundation.
This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
Schmidt Sciences.
Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy.
This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
The US National Science Foundation.
This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society.
For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.
Institutions
Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:
Space Telescope Science Institute.
STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
Wellcome Sanger Institute.
One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
The Francis Crick Institute.
Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences.
One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
EMBL.
The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
Gladstone Institutes.
An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
Research projects and initiatives
As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:
FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience).
It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system).
Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research).
Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease).
The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
Tau Ceti (mathematics).
This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
Centre for Population Genomics.
A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.
As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Monthly API credits for Max, Ultra, and Team plans
Updated over a week ago
Copy for LLM
Max, Ultra, and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max
$100
Ultra
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max, Ultra, or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max or Ultra:
to be the subscriber
Team:
to be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max or Ultra subscriber, or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max to Ultra.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max or Ultra to Team.
Your Max or Ultra link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max, Ultra, or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

A gravity-compensation loop built from three custom Holoscan operators reads joint state at 400 Hz, computes inverse dynamics with
Pinocchio
, and sends torque commands to the
Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM
using the motorbridge library.
Holoscan partitions group the operators on one thread to avoid cross-thread handoffs, and drop-oldest queues prevent outdated samples from accumulating.
Nsight Systems profiling with built-in NVTX annotations shows pinning the control partition to a CPU core reduces p99.99 latency by roughly 5x for C++ and 9.6x for Python implementations.
Next Steps
Download the
Holoscan 5 SDK
to begin developing robotic control applications.
Follow the
gravity compensation tutorial
to build and run the complete example on supported hardware.

Learn more
Picture guiding a robot arm by hand while its motors supply just enough torque to support its weight and keep the robot upright. This simple interaction, a useful starting point for robots that learn by demonstration, manipulate objects, or work alongside people, depends on a gravity-compensation loop.
Building such a loop is only possible by continuously calculating the inverse dynamics of the system based on precise models of all the links of the robot arm, their dimensions, masses, and moments of inertia. This calculation, which needs to be done rapidly with low jitter, requires knowing the current state of the robot, so gravity-comp demos are an excellent proof of life for both the robot model and the runtime that’s executing these algorithms.
NVIDIA Holoscan 5
introduced robotic control alongside streamlined sensor processing. In this tutorial, we’ll build custom Holoscan SDK operators and wire them into a graph. We’ll test the code on a real robot and use the Holoscan SDK’s built-in Nsight Systems annotations to inspect latency and jitter.
This walkthrough has been tested on Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson Thor, and x86 Ubuntu 24.04 systems.
Why Holoscan?
Video 1. A responsive robot with Holoscan installed for gravity compensation workload vs. a custom script runtime
Holoscan SDK brings low-latency control and high-throughput perception into one programming model
, with execution paths designed for CPU- and GPU-based workloads. Its goal is a transparent runtime: minimize avoidable framework overhead while making application execution explicit and inspectable.
Keep the control path focused on the work.
Holoscan uses partitions to group chains of operators on a single thread, avoiding cross-thread handoffs and unnecessary syscalls, reducing latency and jitter. Clock and data-arrival triggers express when work should run, while bounded, drop-oldest queues prevent outdated work from accumulating.
Bring existing algorithms and code rather than rewriting them for a framework.
Holoscan 5 has a new, lightweight programming model that can be easily integrated into existing code bases, and it’s never been easier to get data into and out of Holoscan graphs.
Add perception without adopting a different programming model.
Whether you’re handling 10 kHz CPU-centric motor control loops, heavy-throughput GPU algorithms, or AI inference, Holoscan lets developers and their agents clearly express execution intent using the same operators, ports, and graph APIs, logically splitting their workloads into separate graphs that can coexist, with the ability to pin partitions to dedicated CPU cores, CUDA green contexts, or even execute as a CUDA graph.
Inspect the plan, then measure the result.
Operators express their intent with timing contracts, and before the first run, the compiled plan exposes how the application will execute and catches configuration errors before deployment. This means agents and developers can quickly iterate on a design without ever deploying to real hardware. Plus, built-in NVTX annotations make operator execution and message transfers visible in Nsight Systems. Developers can examine host control-path latency and update jitter, then repeat those measurements as the application grows.
An accessible platform for torque-control development
This tutorial is built around the
Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM
, which is an accessible, affordable platform for getting started with modern robotics control. Most low-cost robot arm development platforms use highly-geared hobby servos, which are only suitable for positional control. The reBot Arm uses quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators that provide high torque bandwidth for both control and sensing — important for haptic, co-bot, or other torque-oriented projects like this one.
Starting off with gravity-comp
Before adding perception pipelines, motion planners, and other higher-level controls, building a basic gravity compensation loop helps provide a useful (and entertaining!) sanity-check for whether your simulation model accurately describes the physical robot. While position-control examples can mask problems with joint axes, offsets, link placements, masses, and moments, all of these affect the required torque in instantly-observable ways; any bugs in DH parameters or mass properties can make the arm sag or push upward as its pose changes.
Even if your end application doesn’t need gravity-comp, torque control lets us shape how the robot responds to forces—a key ingredient in safer interaction between humans and co-bots. Our arm combines gravity feedforward with light stiffness and damping, so it supports its weight while yielding to a person’s hand.
That flexibility makes timing critical. Tracking a position through torque commands requires rapid, consistent feedback at hundreds or thousands of Hz, and runtime overhead and thread handoffs can add phase lag and jitter that cause the robot to become unstable.
This tutorial uses
Pinocchio
as the inverse-dynamics solver. It loads the robot’s URDF model and provides a Recursive Newton–Euler Algorithm (RNEA) solver, which calculates joint torques for specified positions, velocities, and accelerations. We also use the
motorbridge
library to read joint feedback and send commands to the arm’s motors.
Set up the Python example
This walkthrough uses Holoscan’s Python API. The tutorial repository also contains a complete
C++ implementation
, with its own
build instructions
. Both implement the same three-operator control loop.
Use Python 3.12 or newer on Linux. From the repository root:
python3.12 -m venv build/python-venv
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip install --only-binary=:all: -r requirements-python.txt
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip check
Check the serial device and motor IDs in the arm’s configuration file. The tutorial repository’s technical guide covers configuration, the math, and hardware startup.
Express the control loop as three operators
Holoscan 5 has two programming concepts: Operators and Graphs. To read the robot’s state, calculate the command using the inverse-dynamics solver, and send it to the arm, we can decompose that problem into three operators wired into a graph:
Figure 1. Closed loop control system diagram
Operators are subclassed from
Operator
and have three important methods to implement:
Method
Purpose
setup()
Declare input and output ports.
contract()
Declare when to run and which input data to use.
compute()
Read input(s), do work, and publish output(s).
Table 1. Core methods to implement for custom Holoscan operators
Here are outlines of the three operators to build:
1. Read joint state on a clock
JointStateSourceOp
declares one output in
setup()
. Its
OnClock
contract requests a tick every 2.5 ms (we’re running this demo at 400 Hz). Each
compute()
reads all seven motors and emits their state:
import holoscan as hsdk
class JointStateSourceOp(hsdk.Operator):
state = hsdk.Output("state", hsdk.pyobject)
def setup(self, spec):
spec.output(self.state)
def contract(self):
return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnClock(period=hsdk.time.us(2500)))
def start(self):
self.sequence = 0
def compute(self, ctx):
self.sequence += 1
self.state.emit(robot.read_state(self.sequence))
2. Compute gravity compensation when state arrives
PinocchioGravityOp
declares a state input and command output.
OnEach
runs it when state arrives. The
hsdk.Param
declarations expose gains, torque scaling, and joint direction as operator parameters:
class PinocchioGravityOp(hsdk.Operator):
state = hsdk.Input("state", hsdk.pyobject)
command = hsdk.Output("command", hsdk.pyobject)
kp = hsdk.Param(1.5, range=(0.0, 500.0))
kd = hsdk.Param(1.0, range=(0.0, 5.0))
tau_scale = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)
joint_direction = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)
def setup(self, spec):
spec.input(self.state, queue_depth=1)
spec.output(self.command)
def contract(self):
return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.state))
def compute(self, ctx):
state = self.state.receive_data()
command = controller.compute(
state, kp=self.kp, kd=self.kd,
tau_scale=self.tau_scale, joint_direction=self.joint_direction)
self.command.emit(command)
compute()
passes the observed state and current parameters to a helper that maps the six arm angles into the URDF model, checks limits, and obtains gravity torques through Pinocchio:
gravity = pin.computeGeneralizedGravity(self.model, self.data, self.q)[self.v_indices]
Its torques become feedforward in the motors’ commands, alongside position, velocity, stiffness, and damping. The arm uses gravity feedforward and the configured compliant gains from the first command.
3. Send each command to the motors
MotorCommandSinkOp
declares one input and runs whenever a command arrives.
compute()
hands the command to a small robot helper, which rejects expired, out-of-order, or out-of-range commands before sending the batch:
class MotorCommandSinkOp(hsdk.Operator):
command = hsdk.Input("command", hsdk.pyobject)
def setup(self, spec):
spec.input(self.command, queue_depth=1)
def contract(self):
return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.command))
def compute(self, ctx):
robot.send_command(self.command.receive_data())
def stop(self):
robot.disable()
After sending all seven motor commands, the helper records the completion time. If no batch completes for 100 ms (the default timeout), the application’s watchdog attempts to disable the motors and stops the graph. The operator’s
stop()
callback also disables the motors.
Wire, compile, prepare, and run
The application connects the operators through their ports and supplies the gravity parameters when creating the operator:
graph = hsdk.Graph("rebot-gravity", default_clock=hsdk.RealtimeClock)
source = graph.op(JointStateSourceOp, "joint_feedback")
gravity = graph.op(PinocchioGravityOp, "gravity", **controller.parameters.operator_kwargs())
sink = graph.op(MotorCommandSinkOp, "motor_commands")
graph.add_flow(source.state, gravity.state, queue_depth=1, queue_policy=hsdk.QueuePolicy.DROP_OLDEST)
graph.add_flow(gravity.command, sink.command, queue_depth=1, queue_policy=hsdk.QueuePolicy.DROP_OLDEST)
graph.partition("control").add(source).add(gravity).add(sink)
A partition groups operators whose callbacks execute serially on one runtime-owned thread. Keeping all three in
control
avoids thread handoffs between reading state, calculating torque, and sending commands. The source sets the pace; the other operators follow the data. Depth-one, drop-oldest queues keep old samples from piling up.
Holoscan compiles this description into an inspectable execution plan before we enable the motors:
plan = hsdk.compile(build_graph(robot, controller))
if not plan:
raise RuntimeError(plan.summary())
prepare_gravity_compensation(robot, controller)
hsdk.run_async(plan)
Model and motor initialization live in
prepare_gravity_compensation()
, after graph compilation and immediately before execution. The application’s signal handlers set
stop_requested
on Ctrl+C; the main loop supervises command progress, and the session context manager stops and joins the graph. The
control policies
cover startup, watchdogs, and shutdown.
See the arm respond
Start with the arm in its power-off-safe home position:
build/python-venv/bin/python python/gravity_compensation.py
When
Gravity compensation active
appears, guide the arm by hand. Return it home manually before pressing Ctrl+C, which disables the motors.
Video 2. The controller updates while the joint torques as the pose changes
Measure latency and jitter with Nsight Systems
Holoscan has seamless integration with NVIDIA Nsight Systems, giving you powerful tools for analyzing real-world system behavior for both GPU- and CPU-based workloads.
NVIDIA Nsight Systems
. No tracing decorators or custom timing code are needed, simply profile the unmodified application:
mkdir -p build/profiles
nsys profile -t nvtx --sample=none --backtrace=none --cpuctxsw=none \
-o build/profiles/gravity-python \
build/python-venv/bin/python python/gravity_compensation.py
Open the timeline:
Figure 2. NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys) timeline and NVTX event trace showing task timing and latency across operators
You can also calculate a standard range summary:
nsys stats --report nvtx_sum build/profiles/gravity-python.nsys-rep
Pinning cores
Holoscan’s deployment API lets us pin the control partition to a CPU. For these runs, we put helper and profiler threads on another CPU, then used a temporary Linux cgroup to reserve both physical cores, including their SMT siblings, from other applications. This is a simple setup that needs no kernel rebuild, boot-parameter changes, or reboot, but interrupts, timers, and some kernel threads can still run on those cores.

Speed Up Image Generation with FLUX 3 Image Klein on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs

By

and

AI-Generated Summary
FLUX 3 Image Klein Base
and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution.
TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200.
Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x.
Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033.
Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x.
Next Steps
Run the
FLUX 3 example
to execute end-to-end inference with the provided YAML configurations.
Explore the
TensorRT LLM VisualGen runtime and optimization utilities
to understand the optimization APIs.
File issues or share results on the
TensorRT LLM GitHub
to engage with the development team.

Learn more
When deploying diffusion models in design tools, image editors, and visual production workflows, developers must account for inference latency. Generating an image requires multiple sequential passes through a model with billions of parameters, and higher resolutions increase attention costs.
FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers
Base
and
distilled
checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.
This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.
FLUX 3 inference with TensorRT LLM VisualGen
FLUX 3 Image Klein combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer (DiT) to refine image latents, and an autoencoder to decode latents into images and encode I2I reference inputs. Klein processes text, noisy target-image, and optional reference-image streams independently before combining them through joint attention.
TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization.
Figure 1 compares outputs at 2048×2048. The summarized T2I prompt describes a kitchen still life; the summarized I2I prompt requests changes to a space scene, including a red gas giant, a silver dragon, and an engraved plaque.

Figure 1. BF16 and NVFP4 outputs for T2I and I2I
Figure 2. FLUX 3 Image Klein generation latency
With NVFP4 as the starting point, VisualGen optimizations turned to denoising, which dominates overall generation time on B200. Accelerating FLUX 3’s DiT is therefore the focus of the following sections.
Table 1 shows pipeline latency at 2048×2048 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU using NVFP4, VANILLA attention, and torch.compile. Results are averaged over 10 requests after two warmup requests. Base uses 50 denoising steps with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 steps without CFG.

Optimizing FLUX 3 in TensorRT LLM VisualGen
TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates NVFP4 DiT inference with optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels and epilogue fusion, low-precision and sparse attention, caching, and multi-GPU execution. Unless otherwise noted, the following benchmarks use
torch.compile
and seed 0. Base uses 50 denoising steps and a CFG scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 denoising steps.
NVFP4 inference
VisualGen supports BFL’s prequantized NVFP4 DiT checkpoints for
FLUX 3 Image Klein
and
FLUX 3 Image Klein Base
. To use these checkpoints, set
variant
to
nvfp4
in
pipeline_config
:
pipeline_config:
variant: nvfp4
GEMM kernel optimization
TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS
Primitives
and
Task Scheduling
to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See
FlashInfer PR #5758
for more details.
At launch, the pinned NVFP4 PrimsTS kernels delivered 1.02–1.10x faster T2I generation on B200 than the autotuned TensorRT LLM NVFP4 GEMM implementation.
Figure 3. T2I latency with PrimsTS and TensorRT LLM GEMMs
Quantized and sparse attention
Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with
cuDNN FP8
or
VC-Attention
FP8, and sparse attention with
Sol-Attention
. VC-Attention FP8 is a TensorRT LLM variant of the method described in the
VC-Attention paper
.
Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) measures perceptual differences between generated images. In the following comparisons, lower scores indicate greater similarity to the corresponding VANILLA baseline output.
Compared with VANILLA BF16 attention, cuDNN FP8 delivered generation speedups of 1.08x for Base and 1.09x for the 16-step distilled Klein. The corresponding LPIPS scores were 0.072 and 0.161. VC-Attention FP8 delivered speedups of 1.18x for Base and 1.16x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
Figure 4 compares FLUX 3 Image Klein Base NVFP4 outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled.
These measurements suggest using VC-Attention FP8 for quantized attention at 2048×2048 on B200. The tested configuration uses a repair budget of ρ=0.005 to select the fraction of tokens with the highest quantization error for residual correction. To use quantized attention, replace
attention_config
with one of the following configurations:
For cuDNN FP8:
attention_config:
backend: CUDNN
quant_attention_config:
qk_dtype: fp8
v_dtype: fp8
For VC-Attention FP8:
attention_config:
backend: TRTLLM
quant_attention_config:
qk_dtype: fp8
v_dtype: fp8
vc_attention: true
vc_repair_budget: 0.005
Tea scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000
Tea scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.072
Tea scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.086
Cat scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000
Cat scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.066
Cat scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.049
Figure 4. BF16, cuDNN FP8, and VC-Attention FP8 example outputs
Sol-Attention reduces DiT computation with sparsity controlled by τ. The reported tests use the PrimsTS-based general block-sparse attention kernel in TensorRT LLM. Configure Sol-Attention as follows:
attention_config:
backend: TRTLLM
sparse_attention_config:
algorithm: sol_attn
tau: 1.0
disabled_until_timestep: 0.96
For NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base at 2048×2048 on B200, Sol-Attention with τ=1.0 delivered 1.24x faster denoising plus autoencoder decoding than compiled dense VANILLA with 16 initial dense steps, or 1.30x with 12.
These measurements suggest using 16 initial dense steps to prioritize fidelity or 12 to prioritize speed. Higher τ reduced output quality with little additional speedup.
Figure 5 compares NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled and τ=1.0.

Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 16 dense steps · 1.235x · LPIPS 0.075
Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 12 dense steps · 1.297x · LPIPS 0.151

Figure 5. Dense attention and Sol-Attention outputs with 16 or 12 initial dense steps
Step caching
Cache-DiT reduces FLUX 3 Image Klein inference latency by reusing intermediate transformer outputs across denoising steps without retraining or modifying model weights. A residual-difference threshold controls when cached outputs are reused, so you can adjust the balance between inference speed and output quality. Configure Cache-DiT with your desired parameters:
cache_config:
cache_backend: cache_dit
Fn_compute_blocks: 1
Bn_compute_blocks: 0
max_warmup_steps: 4
max_continuous_cached_steps: 3
residual_diff_threshold: 0.24
At a threshold of 0.24, Cache-DiT nearly halved NVFP4 Base T2I latency at both tested resolutions, with smaller gains for the distilled Klein. At 1024×1024, speedups were 1.97x for Base and 1.26x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.038 and 0.036 against their respective uncached outputs. At 2048×2048, speedups were 1.94x for Base and 1.20x for distilled Klein (Figure 6).
Base without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0.000
Base with Cache-DiT · 1.94x · LPIPS 0.033
Distilled Klein without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0
Distilled Klein with Cache-DiT · 1.20x · LPIPS 0.022
Figure 6. Base and distilled Klein outputs with and without Cache-DiT
Multi-GPU inference
The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone.
VisualGen handles sequence splitting, distributed attention, and output gathering. For eight-GPU NVFP4 Base inference, use the following configuration:
parallel_config:
cfg_size: 2
ulysses_size: 4
For the distilled model, set
cfg_size: 1
,
ulysses_size: 8
, and use the
flux-3-image-klein
checkpoint.
At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains.
Figure 7. FLUX 3 Image Klein multi-GPU scaling
At smaller resolutions, CUDA Graphs complement parallelism by reducing kernel-launch overhead as work per GPU shrinks. In a separate 1024×1024 NVFP4 experiment on eight B200s with VANILLA attention, adding CUDA Graphs to compilation reduced Base latency from 1.823 to 0.809 seconds (2.25x, CFG across two GPU groups with Ulysses across four GPUs per group) and distilled latency from 0.791 to 0.366 seconds (2.16x, Ulysses across eight GPUs). Enable CUDA Graphs with the following configuration:
cuda_graph_config:
enable: true
FLUX 3 end-to-end performance
At 2048×2048, Figure 8 compares end-to-end generation speedups across successive TensorRT LLM VisualGen optimization stages against uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference.
On a single B200, compilation, NVFP4 with PrimsTS GEMMs, Sol-Attention, and Cache-DiT delivered a 3.46x generation speedup for T2I, reducing latency from 22.36 to 6.46 seconds, and a 4.45x speedup for I2I, reducing latency from 54.64 to 12.28 seconds. The 16-step distilled Klein achieved up to 2.34x end-to-end speedups.
On a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, compilation, NVFP4 with fused CuTe DSL kernels, and Cache-DiT delivered 1.73-3.25x generation speedups, extending the gains across both platforms. Figures 9 and 10 compare example outputs across optimization stages.

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
- Google Developers Blog
What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
NOV. 9, 2026
Sujeeth Jinesh
Software Engineer
Shaurya Gupta
Software Engineer
Luke Baumann
Software Engineer
Monica Song
Product Manager
Ivan Nardini
AI Developer Relations
Akanksha Gupta
Software Engineer
Anthony Owusu
Software Engineer
Jing Yang
Software Engineer
Sadi Kneipp
Software Engineer
Yu Li
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
TLDR
Today, we announce the General Availability of
Pathways on Google Cloud Platform
. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.
Most large-model training runs as Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programs. Every accelerator runs the same program in lockstep and coordinates through collectives like AllReduce.
It works well when your job is the same program running on every device. It struggles when the job is no longer uniform, like a pipeline whose stages wait on each other or an RL loop where a sampler, a reward model, and a trainer are different programs that have to overlap.
Large runs also have to survive hardware failures, which interrupted
Gemini 2.5 training multiple times per hour
. In SPMD, one lost machine stops every process and sends the run back to its last checkpoint. In each case, the challenge is coordination. You have to decide what runs where and in what order, how tensors move between devices, and how the job keeps going when a machine drops out.
In this post of the series “Pathways on Google Cloud”, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. The post discusses how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.
By the end, you'll know where SPMD is suboptimal, what single-controller execution changes, and how Pathways coordinates a whole training job across a cluster.
When scaling becomes a coordination problem
If you train PyTorch models, you almost certainly use
Distributed Data Parallel (DDP)
or
Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)
. DDP runs a copy of your script on every accelerator and averages gradients with a collective operation such as AllReduce. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers so that the model fits at all.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 1: One training step with DDP and with FSDP.
DDP and FSDP both follow the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model. Every process runs the same copy of your script, owns its accelerators for the whole run, and moves in lockstep with the others, because the only way they coordinate is through collectives like AllReduce. Inside one tightly connected group of accelerators those collectives run over a fast interconnect and are cheap. Scale the job across groups and the same collectives cross the datacenter network, which is far slower. On a
TPU v5p
, for example, each chip gets 1,200 GB/s of bidirectional chip-to-chip bandwidth inside its group, but only 50 Gb/s (gigabits, about 6 GB/s) to the datacenter network which is roughly two orders of magnitude less.
And because every step blocks on its collectives, that communication lands directly in step time. The more groups you span, the larger the share of each step spent moving data, so throughput grows slower than the number of accelerators you add.
As long as your training job is one program that fills the hardware you give it, this execution model fits well. You write your model as if there were one device, and the collectives do the rest. But fitting a model into memory is only part of the problem. Keeping every accelerator busy is the harder part, and this is where the SPMD model starts to show its limits.
Take
pipeline parallelism
as an example. You split a model into blocks across devices, and each device now runs different code over smaller micro-batches. Activations flow forward, activation gradients flow back, and while device 0 works on the first micro-batch, devices 1 and 2 wait. Apart from the idle accelerators you keep paying for, this drops utilization and throughput, even though every device has work in the steady state.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 2: Three devices, four micro-batches. The hatched slots are the pipeline bubble.
Another example is RL post-training for an LLM. You have a sampler that generates rollouts, a reward model that scores them, and a trainer that updates the policy and sends the new weights back to the sampler. These are three different programs that should overlap; otherwise the sampler is idle while the trainer runs, and the trainer is idle while the sampler generates.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 3: The same RL loop, run one after another and overlapped (toy schedule).
In both scenarios, the job is now several different programs running on different devices, and their dependencies can no longer be managed through a single collective. You now have to coordinate which devices share which tensors, which processes run while others are still finishing, and how early to enqueue the next buffer so an accelerator never waits for input. Because each worker only has visibility into its local devices and data, no individual process can manage all of these dependencies itself. That has several consequences.
First, because each process owns its accelerators for the whole run and every collective blocks until all devices finish, one failed machine prevents the collective from completing and stops the entire job, forcing a restart from the last checkpoint. You cannot add devices mid-run, and you cannot give devices back.
Second, because each process holds its accelerators from start to finish, capacity can't move to where it's needed. Within one job, a stage that needs fewer chips than another still keeps the extra ones. They sit idle, you keep paying for them, and no other part of the job can use them until the run ends. Across a team, the same happens at cluster scale. Every job owns its accelerators for as long as it runs, so sharing a cluster means splitting it into per-job allocations, and each new job brings up its own processes on its own hosts.
Finally, the development process itself gets harder. On one host you iterate fast because you run the script, drop into a Python shell, set a breakpoint, and debug. This is not true once the job spans many hosts. You need a launcher to push your script to every host, you hit coordination bugs that never showed up on one machine, and there's no single process to break into. When something hangs, each worker is stuck at a collective waiting for the others, with no one place that shows the whole job.
So the common challenge here is the coordination itself. As soon as the job stops being one program in lockstep, you have to decide what runs where, in what order, and how tensors get from one device to the next.
One way to describe this is as a graph, where each block is a node, each tensor that moves between blocks is an edge, and the devices are where the nodes are placed. You can wire that graph up by hand in SPMD, one process at a time. But what if a single client declared that graph, including what each block does, what it needs, and where it runs, and a distributed runtime handled the transfers, dependencies, and ordering along its edges?
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 3: The same RL loop, run one after another and overlapped (toy schedule).
That is the idea behind
Pathways
, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs
JAX
programs on
TPUs
and it is
available on Google Cloud
.
Coordinating the entire computation with Pathways
With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 5: Virtual devices, the resource manager, and a remap after a host failure.
Because your code refers to virtual devices rather than physical ones, the runtime is flexible to allow users to change the devices used for a given computation. This allows you to stay in control while the runtime handles the mapping to hardware. In an RL loop, for example, the trainer and the samplers rarely want the same number of chips, so you can give the sampler stage more chips by asking for more virtual devices.
Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for
elastic training
. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.
The resource manager owning the chips also means one Pathways cluster can serve several clients, so researchers on a team can share its capacity. With the
Shared Pathways Service
, the cluster stays up as a long running service, which lets you develop interactively on TPUs hosted on GKE. Each client connects on demand from a laptop or VM, gets its own slices (groups of tightly connected TPU chips) from the shared pool, and hands them back when it disconnects. When every chip is busy, the next workload waits until capacity frees up.
Take the three-block model from Figure 2. Block A runs on one group of devices, block B on a second, block C on a third. You declare what each block computes, its target devices, and where its outputs go. Pathways expresses those dependencies as a distributed dataflow graph, in which each block is a compiled SPMD program and each edge is a tensor the runtime has to deliver.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 6: The distributed dataflow graph. Solid arrows cross groups; dashed edges stay local.
In a single SPMD program, the framework handles the collectives that keep the devices in sync within a group, with or without Pathways, and your code doesn't change. The difference shows up once the job runs several programs on different groups (Multiple Programs, Multiple Data, MPMD), like these three blocks or the sampler, reward model, and trainer of an RL loop. Then no single process sees both sides (the same limit from before, where each worker only knows its own devices), so getting a tensor from block A to block B is a hand-off you have to coordinate yourself.
Pathways closes that gap. You declare the dependency once, and the runtime moves and reshards the tensor for you, over the fast interconnect within a group and over the datacenter network between groups.
To keep the accelerators busy, Pathways prepares launches ahead of time with futures and parallel asynchronous dispatch. While block A is still computing, block B can't run yet, but its input shapes and dtypes are already known, so the runtime allocates B's buffers and schedules the transfer before A's output even exists. Host-side setup for every block happens up front, and each block launches when its inputs arrive.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 7: Sequential setup versus asynchronous dispatch (illustrative durations).
This is also what keeps the single client from becoming a bottleneck. Because dispatch is asynchronous, the coordination work overlaps with the compute already running on the chips, so the client stays off the critical path instead of stalling the accelerators between steps.
In Pathways, the runtime decides execution order when a group has more than one operation ready. In pipelined training, B's devices often hold both the forward pass for an upcoming micro-batch and the backward pass for an earlier one. If each device picked on its own, their collectives would conflict and the group would stall.
Pathways has a central scheduler that puts every program's operations into one consistent order, so operations that must communicate start together instead of deadlocking.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 8: Without a shared order the group stalls; with one scheduler it keeps moving.
And because it's still one client, the development loop we mentioned before comes back. It's the same single Python process whether you drive one host or thousands of hosts, so you can
drop into a shell
, set a breakpoint, and inspect the run as it goes. When something stalls, there's one place that knows what's queued on every device and which dependency hasn't been met, instead of a hang spread across separate processes.
Put together, Pathways separates model building from execution. You choose how the model partitions across hardware using the client. And the runtime handles the transfers, ordering, and scheduling that keep accelerators busy, across the whole cluster rather than just your slice of it.
Described this way, Pathways can start to sound like an orchestrator you already know. If scheduling work, moving tensors, and keeping a whole cluster busy brings Ray to mind, it should. But the two work at different layers.
Isn't this what Ray does?
Ray
is an open-source framework for orchestrating Python-native AI workloads across large clusters. It provisions the cluster, schedules your Python code as
tasks and actors
, and launches your workload across hosts, holding data loading, training, serving, and tuning under one control plane. To Ray, an accelerator is a resource to schedule.
What Ray doesn't change is how your training runs on the chips. The job inside each worker
still runs as SPMD
. The framework inserts the collectives, and each process sees only its own devices. Ray places and starts that job but it doesn't turn it into a single program that drives the whole cluster.
That is the layer Pathways works at. It changes the execution model underneath, so one client coordinates every chip. Because they sit at different layers, the two are complementary. In principle, Ray can orchestrate the cluster and the pipeline while Pathways handles how the training step executes.
So concretely, Ray's job is about orchestration while Pathways' job is about execution. With Ray, you tie your data, training, serving, and tuning together and spread heterogeneous work across accelerators and clouds. With Pathways, you run one model across many groups of chips, express patterns beyond SPMD, and recover from a failed host instead of relaunching the whole job.
Conclusion and next steps
When a training job stops being one uniform program, the challenge becomes coordinating the dependencies between stages, the tensors that cross the network, and the ordering that keeps every accelerator fed.
SPMD requires you to address these dependencies. With Pathways, you describe the computation once, from a single client, as a graph of blocks and the tensors between them. And you have a runtime that places the blocks on virtual devices, moves and reshards the tensors, orders the work across the cluster, and remaps around a failed host.
With Pathways, model building and execution are separated and you reason about the whole cluster instead of one slice of it.
If you are curious to learn more about Pathways, you can take a look at the following resources:
Pathways on Google Cloud -
Documentation
Pathways: Asynchronous Distributed Dataflow for ML -
Paper
Resilient training with Pathways -
Documentation
Pathways utils -
GitHub repository
MaxText -
GitHub repository
Happy building!

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs
items.content:
Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
- Google Developers Blog
Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
NOV. 9, 2026
Michael Tran
Software Engineering Intern
Google Cloud
Nuojin Cheng
Software Engineer
Google Cloud
Deepak Patil
Group Product Manager
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.
In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:
Attention Compute:
At long context, attention FLOPs grow quadratically with sequence length and attention dominates the training step. Throughput depends on the attention kernel.
Memory and Communication:
Activations, including the aggregate volume of keys and values for every token, grow with sequence length. Replicating them on every chip, as a naive all-gather does, exhausts high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and triggers out-of-memory failures. In addition, memory-related constraints force communication and recomputation which could negatively impact Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU). The fix here is context parallelism (CP) that streams keys and values instead of materializing them in full.
Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in
MaxText
, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on
Cloud TPU
:
All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention)
, and the
A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP)
, combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the
Tokamax Splash Attention kernel
. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving
70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU)
on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining
50% MFU
across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.
This functionality is available today in
MaxText v0.2.4
(
doc
).
Context Parallelism in MaxText
Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.
Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).
All-gather:
Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 1. All-gather, for one sequence split across four devices (TPU chips). Every device collects all keys and values, then attends locally. Outlined blocks mark attention being computed; small outlined blocks are data in flight.
All-to-All (Ulysses):
Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 2. All-to-All (Ulysses). An all-to-all trades token chunks for attention heads (the rows). Each device attends over the full sequence for its head, and the outputs return with a second all-to-all.
P2P (ring attention):
Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

Figure 3. P2P (ring attention). KV chunks rotate one hop at a time. Each device attends to the chunk it holds while the next one arrives, and holds only one visiting chunk at a time.
A2A + P2P (USP):
A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 4. A2A + P2P (USP). The all-to-all runs within each pair of devices and the P2P ring across the pairs, so each device attends over longer chunks with fewer hops.
These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.
Built on a fast attention kernel
Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from
Tokamax
, Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.
Context Parallelism Strategies and TPU Performance
P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.
TPU v7x (Ironwood) takes the same recipe further. With twice the HBM per chip, P2P training of 14M tokens on 64 TPU 7 chips reached 48.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compared to 37.1% on TPU 5p. We observed that ring attention performs better than other context parallelism strategies -- e.g. Ulysses and USP –- on TPU 7 chips.
Choosing the right strategy
The choice of context parallelism strategy depends mostly on whether the gathered KV fits in HBM, and on how many KV heads the model has:
When the gathered KV fits in HBM:
All-gather, with load balancing on. Its memory grows with the whole sequence, so it is the first to run out, but when it fits, it is the simplest option and was the fastest or near fastest in our runs. The gather can be cheap for grouped-query models, whose KV size is a small fraction of the activations.
On a few chips, up to the number of KV heads:
A2A alone. One all-to-all in, one out, no ring; it does not support multi-query attention.
When the gathered KV no longer fits:
The ring family, whose memory grows with each chip's chunk instead of the whole sequence. We recommend the hybrid (USP) whenever the KV heads allow an A2A factor of 2 or more. Its longer chunks and fewer hops can make it faster than P2P in many settings, keeping pace with all-gather for as long as all-gather fit; the more chips a sequence spans, the more this becomes important. P2P alone remains the choice for MLA models such as DeepSeek, or when the head count doesn't divide.
For all CP strategies, when you run low on memory: Offload before you recompute. MaxText can move saved activations, optimizer states, and parameters to host memory tensor by tensor. At long context lengths, these transfers are hidden behind compute, making offloading effectively free. Offload attention outputs first, followed by optimizer states, layer inputs, parameters, and finally remat as a last resort. MFU stays flat through the offload steps while all-gather falls off and eventually stops fitting. For more details, see the
remat tuning guide
.
What's next
Looking ahead, we see two natural extensions. The first is broader model coverage. Models that mix sliding-window and global layers, such as Gemma, would run the window layers with a short exchange between neighboring chips while the global layers use the ring. We also plan to support linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is performance, with further tuning of the Tokamax kernels and the P2P backward pass to narrow the remaining gap to all-gather at short context, and recipes by model and context length for TPU 5p and 7 chips.
Get started today
Context parallelism is available today in
MaxText v0.2.4
on PyPI, the
corresponding Docker images
and on GitHub main. Sample recipes are available
here
for
TPU 7
and TPU
5p
. Pick a strategy with context_parallel_strategy (ring, ulysses, or usp), set the context-parallel size, and keep the rest of your run the same. The
sharding guide
has the flags and constraints for each strategy, and the
release notes
link to the pull requests behind this work. We can't wait to see what you train.
